title: Area I review: Pilot Privileges and Currency
intro: These questions mix all five Tasks of Area I: the flight review, recent flight experience, medical certificates and BasicMed, pilot documents and notices, and fitness to fly. Many join two of them in one real flight, the way a reviewing instructor would ask.

questions.q: Your last flight review was signed September 18, 2024. In August 2026 a CFI gave you an IPC, and you are now IFR current. It is October 10, 2026, and you want to fly IFR alone. What is true?
options: You may fly IFR, because 61.56 limits only VFR flights with passengers
You may go: the IPC is a proficiency check, so it also replaces the flight review
You may go until October 18, 2026, 24 months to the day after the review
You may not act as PIC at all until you complete a flight review or another 61.56 event
questions.why: The review was good through the end of September 2026, because 61.56(c) counts back to the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month you fly [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. A proficiency check replaces it only when an examiner, an approved check airman or a U.S. Armed Force gives it. An IPC from a CFI is not on that list [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)]]. The IPC did restore instrument currency [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]], but 61.56 limits acting as PIC on any flight. Next time, the instructor may combine the two [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(h)]].

questions.q: You fly under BasicMed with current papers, a current flight review and 90-day passenger currency. Your last 6 approaches, holding and tracking were all in April. On November 14 you want to take two friends IFR at 10,000 ft in a 4-seat single approved for IFR. What is true?
options: You may go: BasicMed allows IFR, and the April tasks count through November
Not IFR yet: first redo the 6 approaches, holding and tracking with a safety pilot, an instructor or a device; no IPC is needed
You may not go: BasicMed pilots may not fly in clouds
Not IFR yet: you need an IPC, because more than 6 months have passed since April
questions.why: BasicMed allows IFR and flight in IMC, but it does not change the need for an instrument rating, instrument currency and an airplane approved for IFR [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.3]]. Two passengers, a 4-seat airplane and 10,000 ft fit the BasicMed limits [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)-(2)]]. For a November flight the window is the 6 calendar months before November, May through October, so the April tasks no longer count [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]. You have been out of currency for less than six calendar months, so you only need to catch up. An IPC is needed only after more than six calendar months out [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]. Counting months from the April date is the common error.

questions.q: You were 41 when you passed a second class exam on February 10, 2026. On March 3, 2027 a local company offers to pay you to fly a pipeline patrol, and a friend asks for a free sightseeing ride. What may you do with that certificate?
options: Both flights, through February 10, 2028
Only the sightseeing ride; commercial privileges ended February 28, 2027
Neither; the certificate expired completely on February 28, 2027
Only the pipeline patrol; second class always covers commercial work
questions.why: Paid flying in an airplane uses commercial privileges and needs at least a second class [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]]. For commercial privileges a second class lasts to the end of the 12th month after the exam month, at any age: February 28, 2027 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(i)]]. For private flying at age 40 or older on the exam date it lasts to the end of the 24th month: February 29, 2028 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(iii)]]. So it did not expire completely; it now covers only the lower privileges [[1:424|PHAK 17-2]].

questions.q: You fly under BasicMed. After a DUI arrest, your State revokes your driver's license on March 1, 2027. What follows?
options: Nothing until a court convicts you; then report within 60 days
Report within 30 days, and you may keep flying on BasicMed with your passport
Report by April 30, 2027, and keep flying under BasicMed until the court decides
Report to the FAA by April 30, 2027, and you can't use BasicMed until the license is reinstated
questions.why: A license revocation for a cause related to driving under the influence is a motor vehicle action by itself, conviction or not [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(c)(2)]]. The written report to AMC-700 is due no later than 60 days after it: March 1 + 60 days = April 30, 2027 [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]]. BasicMed needs a valid U.S. driver's license [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]], and a pilot whose license is revoked can't use BasicMed until it is reinstated [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]]. A passport is good photo ID but can't replace that license [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]]. The 30 days is the address rule [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].

questions.q: You had three beers at a party, the last at 2200. At 0800 a personal breath tester reads 0.02, but you wake with a pounding headache and an upset stomach from last night. You are due to act as PIC at 0830. What applies?
options: You may not go: with a hangover you are still under the influence of alcohol, which 91.17(a)(2) bans
You may go once a pain reliever clears the headache
You may go: more than 8 hours have passed and you are under 0.04
You may not go until a breath test reads 0.00
questions.why: 2200 to 0830 is 10.5 hours, so the 8-hour limit is met, and 0.02 is under 0.04 [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(1)]] [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(4)]]. But all four limits of 91.17(a) apply at once, and one bans acting as a crewmember while under the influence of alcohol [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(2)]]. While you have a hangover you are still under the influence, and motor and mental impairment remain [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]]. A 0.00 reading is not the rule, and there is no way to cure a hangover with a pill [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]].

questions.q: You hold a private pilot certificate with ASEL and a commercial certificate with a balloon rating. In May you complete a satisfactory flight review in a balloon. In July you want to carry a passenger in a Cessna 172. Your last airplane landings were in January. What is true?
options: The balloon review meets 61.56, but you still need 3 takeoffs and landings in an ASEL airplane within 90 days
The balloon review doesn't count for airplanes; you need an airplane flight review
You are legal to carry the passenger, since the review resets all currency
You need both a new airplane flight review and 3 full-stop landings
questions.why: A pilot with several ratings may take the flight review in any aircraft they are rated for, and it meets 61.56 for all of them [[15:24|AC 61-98E 4.2.1.1]] [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. Passenger currency is a separate rule: 3 takeoffs and landings in the preceding 90 days in the same category and class [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]]. January landings are too old for July. Full stops are needed only for a tailwheel airplane [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]]. If you have flown only the balloon lately, the AC says the instructor may recommend an added review in the airplane [[15:24|AC 61-98E 4.2.1.2]].

questions.q: You are 90-day current by day in a Cessna 172. Last week you made 3 touch-and-goes in a tailwheel Citabria. 40 days ago you made 3 full-stop landings in the 172, all more than 1 hour after sunset. Tonight you want to take a friend for a night flight in the Citabria. Are you current?
options: Yes: your night full stops in the 172 cover any single-engine land airplane
Yes: the Citabria touch-and-goes plus the 172 night landings cover it
No: for a tailwheel airplane the 90-day landings must be full stops in a tailwheel airplane
No: night currency must be in the same make and model
questions.why: For a tailwheel airplane, the 61.57(a) landings must be to a full stop in an airplane with a tailwheel [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]]. The touch-and-goes don't count, and the 172 landings are not in a tailwheel airplane. Your 172 night full stops do meet 61.57(b), which asks for same category and class [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]], but you need both rules for passengers at night. Make and model is not part of 61.57 [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]].

questions.q: Your only FAA medical was a third class issued in 2004. Since then you have had a full checkup with your family doctor. You want to fly under BasicMed. What is the first problem?
options: You must have held an FAA medical at some point after July 14, 2006
Your family doctor is not an AME
Your old medical has expired, so it can't be used
BasicMed needs a medical issued within the last 48 calendar months
questions.why: BasicMed requires that, at any point after July 14, 2006, you held a part 67 medical certificate [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(B)]]. A 2004 certificate doesn't meet that, so you need one FAA medical first. That medical may later be expired [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(ii)(B)]]. The doctor does not need to be an AME [[36:19|AC 68-1A 7.1]]. The 48 calendar months is for the comprehensive exam with the CMEC, not for an FAA medical [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(D)]].

questions.q: Your CFI changed her permanent mailing address when she moved 6 weeks ago, and she has not written to the FAA. She offers to give your flight review today. What is the problem?
options: None; she only has to update her driver's license
None; 61.60 applies only to pilot certificates
After 30 days without written notice she may not exercise the privileges of her certificates, so she can't give the review
She may give the ground half only
questions.why: 61.60 covers pilot, flight instructor and ground instructor certificates. After 30 days from the address change, the holder may not exercise the certificate's privileges until written notice reaches the FAA Airman Certification Branch [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]]. Giving flight reviews is a CFI privilege [[60:345|14 CFR 61.193(a)(7)]], and the review must come from an authorized instructor [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. Telling the State is not notice to the FAA.

questions.q: On Thursday at 2000 you take the first dose of an allergy medicine you have never used before. The label warns it may cause drowsiness and says one dose every 4 to 6 hours. You take no more. Using the PHAK rules of thumb, when is the earliest you should fly?
options: Friday 1600: five 4-hour dosing intervals
Saturday 0200: five 6-hour dosing intervals
Saturday 2000: a new medicine also needs 48 hours after the first dose
Friday 0200: one dosing interval, once the dose has worn off
questions.why: Two PHAK rules of thumb apply, and you meet both. For a medicine that may be sedating, wait at least five maximal dosing intervals, so use the longest interval: 5 x 6 = 30 hours, Thursday 2000 to Saturday 0200. For any new medicine, also wait at least 48 hours after the first dose: Thursday 2000 to Saturday 2000 [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. The later time wins. Flying while a drug affects your faculties also breaks 91.17(a)(3) [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]].

questions.q: Your last flight review was November 30, 2024. You passed the practical test for your flight instructor certificate with an examiner on October 1, 2025. It is December 3, 2026. May you act as PIC?
options: Yes; the CFI practical test counts, through October 31, 2027
No; the review ran out November 30, 2026
Yes, but only while giving instruction
Yes, through October 1, 2027 exactly
questions.why: A practical test given by an examiner for a flight instructor certificate replaces the flight review [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)(2)(i)]] [[15:23|AC 61-98E 4.1.2.3.1]]. Your latest qualifying event sets the window. The rule counts calendar months, so October 2025 is good through the end of October 2027 [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. Counting to the exact day is the common error.

questions.q: Your last approaches, holding and tracking were all in January 2026. Your last flight review was December 2024. You did nothing more. In February 2027 you want to fly IFR. You will fly with your usual CFI. What is the least you need?
options: Six approaches, holding and tracking with a safety pilot
An IPC alone, since a CFI's IPC also counts as a flight review
A flight review only; the IFR grace period runs through February
A flight review and an IPC, which the instructor may combine in one session
questions.why: January tasks keep you IFR current through July 2026. August 2026 to January 2027 is the window to catch up without an IPC. By February 2027 you have been out more than six calendar months, so only an IPC restores currency [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]] [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]. The December 2024 review was good through December 31, 2026 [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]], and an IPC from a CFI is not on the 61.56(d) list [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)]]. The instructor may combine the review with 61.57 currency [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(h)]].

questions.q: You are flying under BasicMed with current papers. A friend offers you his single-engine turboprop for a trip at 16,000 ft with 3 passengers. It weighs 7,400 lb at maximum takeoff and is certificated for 9 occupants. May you act as PIC?
options: Yes; you will have only 4 people aboard
No; the airplane is authorized to carry more than 7 occupants
Yes; it is under 12,500 lb and below 18,000 ft
No; BasicMed bans turbine airplanes
questions.why: BasicMed limits the aircraft, not just the people aboard: it must be authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, have a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 lb, and carry no more than 6 passengers [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]. This airplane is authorized for 9, so it is out, even though weight, altitude and passenger count fit [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)(i)]]. The rule says nothing about engine type.

questions.q: After landing at a small field, a State trooper says she is investigating a suspected violation of a State law on flying while intoxicated. State law lets her test. She asks for your pilot certificate and a breath test. What must you do?
options: Show nothing; only the FAA may inspect pilot certificates
Show your certificate, but refuse the test, since only the FAA tests pilots
Take the test, but show your certificate only to an FAA inspector
Show your certificate and photo ID, and submit to the test
questions.why: Any Federal, State or local law enforcement officer may ask to inspect your certificate, and you must present it with your photo ID [[60:193|14 CFR 61.3(l)]] [[60:194|14 CFR 61.3(l)(3)]]. A crewmember must submit to an alcohol test on request when the officer is authorized by State or local law and is investigating that kind of violation [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(c)(1)]]. Refusing is grounds for denial of applications for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.16]] [[60:203|14 CFR 61.16(a)-(b)]].

questions.q: Last night you had two beers, the last at 2300, and slept about 5 hours. Departure is 0730. You feel fine and are sure you are well under 0.04. What is the best answer?
options: The 8-hour limit is met, but alcohol aftereffects and short sleep are pilot hazards; raise your minimums or delay
You are not legal, because the AIM requires 12 hours
You are legal and fit; 8 hours have passed
You are legal only if a breath test reads 0.00
questions.why: 2300 to 0730 is 8.5 hours, so the 8-hour limit is met; you must also be under 0.04 and not under the influence [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. But aftereffects of alcohol can be a pilot hazard for longer than 8 hours, and fatigue comes from too little sleep [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]. The AIM's 12 to 24 hours is advice, not the rule [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1d]]. The RMH example adds at least 500 ft to your ceiling minimum for fatigue [[30:17|RMH Figure 2-9]], and staying home is also an option.

questions.q: According to a study described in the AIH, what was a pilot's memory of the regulations linked to?
options: Total flight hours
Whether the pilot held an instrument rating
The number of months since the pilot's last flight review
The pilot's age
questions.why: The study found pilots' ability to remember details of regulations was related to the months since their last flight review. Pilots tend to sharpen up before a review and let knowledge decay between them [[25:92|AIH 3-41]]. That is why the review should be a real check, not a box to tick every two years, and why a personal currency program that aims past the minimum helps [[15:7|AC 61-98E 1.9.1]].

questions.q: You want to practice approaches under a view-limiting device in a Cessna 172. Which friend may be your safety pilot?
options: A private pilot ASEL flying under BasicMed with a current course and CMEC exam
A private pilot with only a glider rating and a current medical
A student pilot who has passed the instrument knowledge test
A sport pilot with a valid U.S. driver's license
questions.why: The safety pilot must hold at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the aircraft [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]]. That rules out the sport pilot, the student and the glider-only pilot. Because the rule requires a safety pilot, the FAA treats them as a required pilot flightcrew member needing medical qualification [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1]] [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]]. The current rule lets a BasicMed private pilot serve as a required flightcrew member [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]], so the AC's old PIC-only line no longer applies.

questions.q: You are an airline captain. You pass a first class exam on your 40th birthday, May 12, 2026. Through what date does it cover your ATP PIC flying?
options: May 31, 2027, because a first class lasts a year if you are 40 or younger
November 30, 2026
November 12, 2026
questions.why: Your age on the exam date sets the length. At 40 you are "age 40 or older," so for ATP PIC privileges a first class lasts to the end of the 6th month after the exam month: May 2026 + 6 months = November 30, 2026 [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)(1)(ii)]]. The 12 months apply only under age 40 [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)(1)(i)]]. The PHAK line about one year "if the airman is 40 or younger" does not match the rule [[1:424|PHAK 17-2]]. It runs to the end of the month, not to the 12th.

questions.q: You are an airline first officer. Your plastic certificate was lost last week, and your airline gave you a temporary document under its approved certificate verification plan. On your day off you want to rent a Cessna 172. What do you need?
options: Nothing more; the airline's document works for all flights in the U.S.
A photo of the old certificate on your phone
A temporary authority document from the FAA under 61.29(e), since the airline document covers only flights for the airline
Only your photo ID and medical
questions.why: An operator's temporary document counts only when you are engaged in a flight operation within the United States for that part 121 or 135 certificate holder [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)(v)]]. For your own flying, request a duplicate and a temporary authority document, which may be carried for up to 60 days [[60:212|14 CFR 61.29(e)]]. A phone photo is not on the 61.3(a)(1) list [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)]]. Remember the landings too: jet landings don't make you current in a single [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]].

questions.q: For months you have had money and job worries. Lately your scan feels slow and you forget radio calls. Your medical is current. What does the FAA guidance say?
options: This sounds like chronic stress; such a pilot is not safe, should not exercise airman privileges and should see a physician
Fly; stress is not a grounding condition, so a valid medical settles it
Fly, but only with an instructor aboard
Fly only on short local flights until the worries pass
questions.why: Chronic stress from things like financial worries or work problems can exceed your ability to cope, and performance falls off fast. Pilots at that level are not safe, should not exercise their airman privileges and should consult a physician [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. The regulations don't list stress as a grounding condition, so you have to judge it yourself [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]. The AIM says to consider delaying flight until the difficulties are resolved [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1f]].

questions.q: Which of these does AC 61-98E NOT list among the maneuvers an instructor should review on every flight review, whatever the pilot's experience?
options: Recovery from unusual attitudes
Slow flight
Spin recognition and avoidance
Chandelles
questions.why: The AC lists takeoffs, stabilized approaches to landings, slow flight, stall recognition and recovery, spin recognition and avoidance, recovery from unusual attitudes, and flight by sole reference to instruments [[15:28|AC 61-98E 4.3.5.4]]. Chandelles are not on that list. Beyond it, the instructor chooses the maneuvers the pilot needs to show safe exercise of the certificate's privileges [[60:236|14 CFR 61.56(a)(2)]].

questions.q: You and a friend plan day VFR hood work with no one else aboard. You are fully current. He wants to log PIC by acting as PIC while he is safety pilot, but his flight review ran out two months ago. What is the right plan?
options: He may act as PIC; the flight review rule applies only when passengers are carried
He may not act as PIC; you act as PIC under the hood and he serves as safety pilot
He may act as PIC if he logs the time as dual received
Neither of you may fly until he gets a flight review
questions.why: No one may act as PIC without a current flight review or a 61.56 substitute [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. Being safety pilot is not acting as PIC, and the safety pilot needs a private certificate with category and class ratings [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]]. You, as sole manipulator, may log PIC [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(e)(1)(i)]]. Because the rules require a second pilot, he may log SIC if he holds the category and class ratings [[60:229|14 CFR 61.51(f)(2)]]. Decide who is PIC before takeoff.

questions.q: Your spouse says you snore loudly and stop breathing at night, and you feel sleepy most afternoons. You hold a third class medical. What is the best step?
options: Nothing; this is ordinary tiredness that coffee fixes
Get evaluated by a sleep medicine specialist; OSA is easily treated and most treatments are acceptable for certification once shown to work
Surrender your medical; sleep apnea is permanently disqualifying
Keep flying; 61.53 covers only conditions an AME has diagnosed
questions.why: Snoring, daytime sleepiness and breathing pauses in sleep are signs of obstructive sleep apnea, which interrupts restorative sleep. The AIM says to be evaluated by a sleep medicine specialist. OSA is easily treated, and most treatments are acceptable for medical certification once you show they work [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1e(4)]]. 61.53 applies when you know or have reason to know of a condition, not only after a diagnosis [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]]. Fatigue may not be apparent until serious errors are made [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1e]].
